rules.why: Pick the best trade available, not the trade you want to take. If you want action, go to Vegas — at least they give you a free room.

glossary.plain: The person on the other side of a smart trade. When a fund wants out of a big position, someone has to buy it — that someone is usually a retail trader chasing the move.
glossary.said: take what somebody else does and make them what we call exit liquidity

glossary.plain: The smallest price increment a contract moves. On full ES a tick is $12.50; on micro ES it's $1.25. Same chart, ten times the consequence.
glossary.said: each tick is $1.25... if you're trading a big contract, they're $12.50

glossary.plain: One-cancels-the-other. You place a stop and a target together; whichever fills first automatically cancels the other. It's how you leave the desk without leaving the position unprotected.
glossary.said: Oco is one cancels the other

glossary.plain: The nearest-expiry contract. Most liquid, tightest spread, cheapest to trade.
glossary.said: I'm assuming you're trading front month contract because they're less expensive

glossary.plain: The prop firm's audition. Hit a profit target under their risk rules and they hand you a funded account. Passing it is a consistency test, not a profit test.
glossary.said: you need to make $3,000 in profit, and there is a computation on that

glossary.plain: Taking partial profit while leaving the rest on. Reduces risk without giving up the whole move.
glossary.said: we took a trim... Or what we call take profit, we call it trim

glossary.plain: A price jump between one bar's close and the next bar's open, leaving empty space on the chart. A gap that fills and can't push higher is a failed gap.
glossary.said: It gapped up, what happened? the gap failed

glossary.plain: A red candle whose body covers the previous green candle entirely. Buyers made a push and sellers erased it inside one bar.
glossary.said: Bearish engulfing candle? Equals what?

glossary.plain: Exponential moving average — a smoothed line weighted toward recent price. Short ones pointing down while a long one goes flat means momentum has turned before price has.
glossary.said: When these are pointing down, That means this can continue down

glossary.plain: Traders on the wrong side who must exit to stop the bleeding. Their forced exits fuel the move against them — which is why price accelerates after a trap.
glossary.said: They trapped the shorts here... Now I'm trapping the lungs up here

insights.title: The market is not neutral toward you
insights.body: His framing of the counterparty is deliberately unfriendly: the best-funded people in finance are on the other side, they don't know you and aren't there to give you anything. The consolation is asymmetry — you're small enough to take a ten-point win and leave, and they aren't.
insights.said: You're small, you're fast, so you can take money from them quickly

insights.title: Volatility is not opportunity when you're new
insights.body: He calls MNQ the automatic money destroyer, and notes gold got contract-size restrictions at prop firms because people were blowing accounts on it. The point isn't that these instruments are bad — it's that tick value multiplies your mistakes at exactly the stage you're making the most of them.
insights.said: I call it the automatic money destroyer

insights.title: Two indicators, on purpose
insights.body: The free TradingView account caps you at two indicators, and he treats that constraint as the lesson rather than a limitation. He says outright he can read the chart without them. The indicators are training wheels you should be able to take off.
insights.said: I don't have to be able to read a chart without this

insights.title: The candle you want to screenshot is the one you should be selling
insights.body: The most exciting bar on the chart — the big green push — is usually the exhaustion, not the start. This is the single most compressed piece of chart-reading in the call.
insights.said: the candle that they want to take a picture of is the candle you should be selling

insights.title: Paper money and real money are different skills
insights.body: His nephew turned roughly $10,000 into $100,000 in six weeks on a paper account, then couldn't make $20 on a live one. Simulator results tell you your read is right; they tell you nothing about whether you can hold the position.
insights.said: Paper money is not the same as real money

insights.title: Why bonds come first, not the index
insights.body: Everything is priced off rates in a fiat system, so he reads the bond market before he looks at a single stock chart. He watches the 10-year specifically because it's the one most tied to mortgages, and therefore to the consumer.
insights.said: Everything in money deals with the bond market

insights.title: Gas is a tax
insights.body: Rising energy costs compress corporate margins, and compressed margins pull the index down. It's a chain of reasoning, not a correlation he memorized — worth being able to reproduce rather than just recite.
insights.said: gas is nothing but a tax

insights.title: Earnings outrank headlines
insights.body: He ignores news almost entirely, with one exception: a large-cap reporting. His stated hierarchy is that if Walmart falls, the market falls, and the only thing that would override it is something on the scale of a war ending, confirmed by both sides.
insights.said: if Walmart falls, the market falls

insights.title: Consistency is the actual product
insights.body: The prop firm isn't buying big days — a $10,000 day at Josh's account size means something went wrong. Weekly expectations, not daily ones, because losing days are expected inside a winning week.
insights.said: there's gonna be days where you make a loss

rules.rule: If you start with wicks, use only wicks.
rules.why: His one stated rule of thumb for drawing. Consistency of anchor, not which anchor, is what he names.

rules.rule: Drag a resistance line to catch the most touches rather than leaving it where you first drew it.
rules.why: The correct line is the one price actually respected. He starts at the previous swing high and pulls it to the most touches.

rules.rule: Treat the trend as intact until price makes a new high above the lines or a new low below them.
rules.why: Until one of those happens, price is still inside the trend and nothing has changed.

rules.rule: Pair trendlines with volume rather than trading them alone.
rules.why: Volume is what separates a real breakout from a poke above that fails.

setups.name: Break and retest
setups.trigger: Price breaks the line, comes back, retests it, and holds. The line flips role — broken resistance becomes support, broken support becomes resistance.
setups.invalidation: NOT GIVEN. He never says what a failed retest looks like or where you would be wrong.
setups.timeframe: any; he demonstrates on weekly and 1h

setups.name: Volume-confirmed breakout
setups.trigger: Sequence: a strong green candle breaking above with volume behind it, then a push back down that still holds above the line, then multiple holds above.
setups.invalidation: A poke above that falls back below is the fakeout. He counts four consecutive fakeouts before the real break.

routine.what: Pick the timeframe. The same method works on all of them; longer timeframes give the more concrete trend.
Choose wicks or bodies and stay consistent.
For support: anchor at a major swing low and extend right through later reaction lows.
For resistance: start at the previous swing high, then drag the line until it catches the most touches.
Count the touches. That count is the strength read.
If the shape that forms is unfamiliar, screenshot the chart into Grok or ChatGPT and ask what pattern it is.

glossary.plain: A line connecting points where price reacted, extended forward. It predicts nothing; it marks where buyers or sellers turned up before, on the assumption they may again.
glossary.said: Essentially just connecting points that react

glossary.plain: The two kinds of trendline. Horizontal is a flat line at one price level; diagonal is sloped, following the trend. Same idea either way.
glossary.said: you have horizontal support and resistance... then you have diagonal

glossary.plain: The thin line above or below a candle's body, marking the extreme price reached before it was rejected. Anchoring to wicks means using those extremes rather than the open/close.
glossary.said: if you start with wicks you want to use only wicks

glossary.plain: One occasion where price reached the line and reacted. Counting touches is how he grades a line's strength.
glossary.said: we got one two three four touches on this

glossary.plain: A local peak or trough — the point price turned around. Trendlines are anchored to these, not to arbitrary points.
glossary.said: you take your previous swing high

glossary.plain: Price returning to a line it has just broken, to see whether the line now holds in its new role.
glossary.said: once we broke out We came back retested it and it's acting as support

glossary.plain: A break through the line that does not hold and falls straight back. The thing volume confirmation is meant to filter out.
glossary.said: a lot of times you can get pokes above and they're not real

glossary.plain: Each peak above the last peak and each trough above the last trough. The definition of an uptrend, and how he reads trend strength.
glossary.said: a higher high then a higher low... that's showing that there's strength on this trend

glossary.plain: Keep it simple, stupid. His closing framing for the whole method.
glossary.said: kiss keep it simple stupid this is how you do that

insights.title: The correct line is the one price respected most
insights.body: The first line you draw is rarely the right one. He anchors at the previous swing high and then drags until the line catches the most touches — the drawing is a search, not a single decision.
insights.said: Take it to your next or to your most touches

insights.title: Trends nest inside trends
insights.body: A multi-year uptrend contained a complete downtrend within it. Which trend you are looking at is a function of which timeframe you chose, so the timeframe decision comes before the drawing.
insights.said: in trends there is going to be More trends

insights.title: Strength is touches times time
insights.body: More touches make a line stronger, and more time spanned strengthens it again. Four touches reaching back to the March 2020 low is his example of a very strong line — the years matter as much as the count.
insights.said: a very strong trend line because it's over multiple years

insights.title: Steep trends are the strongest signal and the least durable
insights.body: A steep downtrend is a strong read on weakness. But his own example then breaks and flattens into sideways grinding, so steepness tells you about the present state rather than how long it lasts.
insights.said: if it's a steep trend down and it's a very strong indicator of weakness

insights.body: When a shape forms that he does not recognise, he screenshots the chart into Grok or ChatGPT and asks what pattern it is. His own suggestion, offered without embarrassment — worth noting because it tells you how he expects a student to close gaps.

rules.rule: Measure a new trend from the impulse move — the lower low, then the lower high that failed to close above the previous high.

call.title: Price Action — The Four-Stage Cycle
call.date_note: CONFIRMED from Discord: posted to #videos by Lige [FLOW] on 25 Nov 2025 at 1:14 PM, captioned 'Price action quick video'. willruss47 replied that day calling it 'great info and very simple to understand'; Lige answered 'im glad I can help'.
call.mentor: Lige — teaching on Jason Murray's behalf and with his approval. Part of the one sanctioned iBelieve Investments Club method.
call.format: recorded lesson video. TrendSpider, LULU (Lululemon) MONTHLY from 2007 to 2026, iBelieve watermark. He draws the stages on live as he talks.
call.instrument_class: Context framework, not an entry method. Demonstrated on a single stock monthly, but he states outright it applies on any timeframe.
call.source: Price_action.mp4 — downloaded from Discord 23 Aug 2026, transcribed with faster-whisper.
call.note: THIS LESSON CONTAINS NO ENTRIES, NO EXITS AND NO STOPS. It is the layer that tells you which stage a chart is in — the context the other lessons' setups sit inside. Do not read a trade out of it.

rules.rule: Read the four-stage cycle from the top down — higher timeframes first.
rules.why: His one procedural instruction in the lesson. Doing it top-down 'will give you a lot more clarity on where your stock is and what it's doing'.

rules.rule: The cycle works on any timeframe.
rules.why: He demonstrates on a monthly spanning nearly twenty years, then says explicitly it is not a monthly-only tool.

rules.rule: Pair the stage read with chart patterns to get at the psychology behind the move.
rules.why: His closing instruction. The stage tells you where you are; the patterns tell you what people are doing inside it.

levels.meaning: price on the day of the lesson, in what he reads as a downtrend heading back toward accumulation — HISTORY, 25 Nov 2025, not a live read

routine.what: STAGE 1 — ACCUMULATION. Follows a sell-off. The stock goes sideways for weeks or months while big money buys cheap shares from people who are panicking. Volume is usually low, volatility contracts, and price coils up.
STAGE 2 — UPTREND. Price breaks out of the accumulation range on INCREASING volume. Higher highs and higher lows. Pullbacks are shallow and quick. He calls this 'the trend is your friend phase'.
STAGE 3 — DISTRIBUTION (the top). Smart money sells to late buyers. Price goes sideways again but with wild swings, higher volume on down days, and fake breakouts in both directions. It looks messy.
STAGE 4 — DOWNTREND. The stock rolls over and makes a lower low. Then the cycle repeats from accumulation.

questions.q: How do you tell distribution from accumulation while you are in it?
questions.why: Both are sideways ranges after a directional move, and he distinguishes them by volume character and swing violence rather than by shape. On a chart with no right-hand side that is a genuinely hard call, and he does not say how to make it in real time.

questions.q: Which stage is ES in, and on which timeframe should Josh be reading it?
questions.why: The lesson is demonstrated on a twenty-year monthly. Josh trades ES on the 1-hour. 'Top down' implies starting higher than his trading timeframe, but nothing says how far up to start or where to stop.

questions.q: Do the setups only work in certain stages?
questions.why: The obvious implication of a context framework is that a breakout setup belongs in stage 2 and a fade belongs in stage 3 — but that is inference, not something he says. Worth asking whether the gap-up short and the hold-above-the-candle long are stage-specific.

glossary.plain: The sideways base after a sell-off where large buyers quietly take shares off panicking sellers. Low volume, shrinking volatility, price coiling.
glossary.said: your stock goes sideways for weeks or months after a big drop. The big money is going to be buying up cheap shares from people that are panicking

glossary.plain: The sideways range at the top where large holders sell to late buyers. Same sideways shape as accumulation but violent — wild swings, heavier volume on down days, fake breakouts both ways.
glossary.said: Smart money starts selling to late buyers and price will go sideways again but now with wild swings and higher volume on down days

glossary.plain: Accumulation, uptrend, distribution, downtrend — then back to accumulation. His whole framing of price action, and it repeats on every timeframe.
glossary.said: Simplify it down to a four-stage cycle that you'll see over and over again in stocks

glossary.plain: Reading the higher timeframe first and working downward, so you know which stage the bigger picture is in before you judge the smaller one.
glossary.said: It's best to start from the top down, so higher time frames down

insights.title: This is the layer underneath every other lesson
insights.body: Trendlines, support and resistance, fibs and the moving-average stack all tell you WHERE something might happen. This tells you WHICH REGIME you are in when it does. A breakout means one thing in stage 2 and something close to the opposite in stage 3, where he says fake breakouts run in both directions. Read this first.
insights.said: it will give you a lot more clarity on where your stock is and what it's doing

insights.title: Accumulation and distribution are the same shape and opposite meanings
insights.body: Both are sideways ranges. What separates them is volume character and how violent the swings are — accumulation is quiet and coiling, distribution is messy with heavier volume on down days. That is the single hardest read in the framework and the one worth practising, because getting it backwards means buying the top while believing you are buying the base.
insights.said: looks messy fake breakouts up and down

insights.title: It is the same idea as exit liquidity, drawn on a chart
insights.body: Jason told Josh that funds getting out of big positions need someone to buy from them, and that someone is usually retail chasing the move — what he called exit liquidity (17 Aug 2026, 03:20). Distribution IS that, made visible: smart money selling to late buyers across weeks. His other line, that the candle people want to screenshot is the candle you should be selling (17 Aug 2026, 30:30), is the same event at candle scale.
insights.said: Smart money starts selling to late buyers

insights.title: Top-down is now settled across three lessons
insights.body: Zoom out when in doubt (Fibonacci Extensions). Zooming out flipped the read from bearish to bullish (Support and Resistance). Start from the top down (here). Three separate videos, same instruction — this is one of the few things in the corpus stated often enough to count as a settled principle rather than a single remark.
insights.said: It's best to start from the top down

insights.title: Volume is the tell at every transition
insights.body: Low volume in accumulation, increasing volume on the breakout, higher volume on down days in distribution. Volume is what he uses to date each stage change — which lines up with the Trendlines lesson, where volume is what separates a real breakout from a poke above that fails.
insights.said: the stock will break out of that range on increasing volume

frames.caption: LULU monthly on TrendSpider. The first accumulation base he marks — the long flat stretch after the 2008 financial crisis, boxed in green.
The break out of that range on increasing volume, and the higher-highs/higher-lows leg he calls the trend-is-your-friend phase.
Marking the first distribution range in red, around 2012-2013 near $60-80 — sideways, but messy compared with the accumulation box below it.
The downtrend leg out of distribution, rolling over into a lower low and back toward the next accumulation.

The finished picture: LULU monthly 2007-2026 with two complete cycles boxed — accumulation after the GFC, the run to ~$450 by 2021, the 2021-2024 distribution range, and the downtrend into 177.48 where he says you would assume accumulation is next. That last read is dated 25 Nov 2025.

call.date_note: CONFIRMED from Discord: posted to #videos by Lige [FLOW] on 21 Nov 2025 at 2:48 PM, captioned 'Support and resistance in under 5 mins on MSFT'.
call.mentor: Lige — Jason Murray's NEPHEW (confirmed by Ifoma, 23 Aug 2026). A second, distinct presenter in the iBelieve Investments Club. He teaches the chart lessons; Jason teaches options/callouts and runs Josh's coaching calls. Attribute this lesson to Lige.
call.format: recorded lesson video, no students present. TrendSpider, MSFT daily then weekly, iBelieve watermark.
call.instrument_class: Chart method on a single stock (MSFT), daily and weekly. Not futures, not options — but unlike the moving-average lesson, the method here is instrument-agnostic and he says so implicitly by moving between timeframes.
call.source: SR_in_Stonks_under_5_mins.mp4 — downloaded from Discord 23 Aug 2026, transcribed with faster-whisper. The opening 'this is Liza' is 'this is Lige' mis-heard, the same artefact as the Trendlines transcript.
call.closes: Answers two questions that were open across the corpus: the touch threshold for a tradeable level, and the invalidation for a broken level that should flip.

rules.rule: More than three touches is the key. That is what makes a level strong.
rules.why: The threshold the corpus has been missing. He is explicit that it must be over a period of time, and NOT read off a shorter-timeframe chart.
rules.answers: Open question from the Trendlines lesson: 'How many touches make a line tradeable rather than merely noticed?' Lige answers it — more than three, over time, on a longer timeframe.

rules.rule: Support and resistance are AREAS, not set prices.
rules.why: His first and most emphasised point. When volatility is up and the VIX is high, price can range through a level by a couple of dollars, sometimes ten or more depending on the name. Treating a level as an exact number is the beginner error.

rules.rule: Know how volatile the stock you are trading is before you use its levels.
rules.why: It follows directly from levels being areas — the width of the area is a function of the instrument.

rules.rule: When support breaks it is supposed to act as resistance. If it does not, it is support again — and the same in reverse.
rules.why: The clearest invalidation statement anywhere in the corpus. It gives the flip a failure condition instead of leaving it as a one-way expectation.
rules.answers: Open question from the Trendlines lesson: 'What invalidates a failed retest?' This is the answer, from Lige rather than Jason — a broken level that fails to hold in its new role reverts to its old one.

rules.rule: If you start with wicks, continue with wicks; if you start with bodies, continue with bodies.
rules.why: Identical to the rule in the Trendlines lesson. Stated twice now, in two separate videos, which makes consistency of anchor one of the few things genuinely settled in the corpus.

routine.what: Establish whether the level is support (a floor where buying meets or exceeds selling) or resistance (a ceiling where selling overcomes buying), using historical price on the chart.
Count the touches and note how long they span. More than three, over a period of time, is what makes it strong.
Treat an all-time-high test as a strong level in its own right — no overhead history means it can signal reversals.
When a level breaks, watch whether it flips role. If it does not, it has not really broken.
Find the next level down (or up) before you need it — for MSFT, the 200-day and the previous all-time highs coincided.
Zoom out to the weekly and draw trendline support and resistance the same way, anchoring consistently on wicks or bodies.

glossary.plain: A price area where a decline may pause because buying interest is strong enough to meet or exceed selling pressure. The floor.

glossary.plain: A price area where a rise may pause because selling pressure overcomes buying interest. The ceiling.
glossary.said: a price level where an increasing price trend may pause because selling pressure is strong enough to overcome buying interest

glossary.plain: A support or resistance level is a zone, not a number. How wide depends on the instrument's volatility and where the VIX is.

glossary.plain: The band between a trendline support and a trendline resistance running parallel. If the top fails, he expects a move back to the bottom of it.

glossary.plain: The same support/resistance logic applied with sloped lines on longer timeframes rather than horizontal levels.

insights.title: Why levels hold is people taking profit
insights.body: His explanation is mechanical rather than mystical: the traders who bought at support are the ones selling at resistance, so the level holds because that is where a cohort of people decided in advance to get out. It reframes a level as a record of other people's decisions rather than a property of the price.
insights.said: A lot of times they got in at support and they're selling at resistance and they're just taking profit

insights.title: A level that breaks and does not flip has not really broken
insights.body: The most useful sentence in the lesson, and the corpus's cleanest invalidation. It turns the flip from something you hope happens into a test you can fail: if broken support does not start capping price, treat it as support still. insights.title: Two independent things landing on the same price is what makes it strong
insights.body: On MSFT he stacks reasons: around 470 the 200-day moving average sits AND the previous all-time highs were there. He does not name the principle, but the behaviour is confluence — a level earns weight when more than one method points at it.

glossary.plain: A trade idea posted in the Discord. It names the security and the direction and deliberately stops there — no strike, no expiration. You do the sizing and selection yourself.
glossary.said: a call-out is simply a trade idea that you can implement into your own investing and trading strategy

glossary.plain: Opening a new option position by buying it. 'Long calls', 'scalp long', 'buy a put', 'short Apple' all resolve to a buy-to-open in his language.
glossary.said: we want to purchase an option or what we call buy to open

glossary.plain: The price at which an option can be exercised. His rule is to take the strike closest to where the stock is trading.
glossary.said: you would use the strike prices closest to the price of the stock

glossary.plain: Weeklies expire every Friday; monthlies expire the third Friday. Weeklies for a quick move, monthlies if you want to be more conservative.
glossary.said: These expire every third Friday. If you're trying to get a move that's very quick, then you want to use the weeklies

glossary.plain: Volume-weighted average price — the average price paid through the session, weighted by volume. He treats which side of it price is on as a pass/fail condition for direction.
glossary.said: Is it above VWAP? Is it above the 9 and the 21 EMA?

glossary.plain: His confirmation level on the 1-hour. Above it supports a long, below it supports a short.
glossary.said: it's above my 50 line. So everything checks out to take this long

glossary.plain: Buy one option and sell a further one in the same direction. Costs money up front, caps the gain, and cuts the cost of the trade. His choice for swings rather than scalps.
glossary.said: a spread is typically for a trade that you're looking to take for more than one day

glossary.plain: Sell the nearer option and buy a further one for protection, taking money in up front. He uses it on the opposite side to help pay for a debit spread.
glossary.said: Now we've created a credit spread instead of a debit spread

glossary.plain: A spread where both legs share an expiration and differ only in strike.
glossary.said: Which would be a vertical put?

glossary.plain: An option whose strike is already on the profitable side of the current price. He avoids putting the short leg of a spread there so the full premium can be collected.
glossary.said: the bottom portion of your actual spread you want to actually not go in the money

glossary.plain: A quick directional trade, in and out. Distinct from a spread, which he holds longer than a day.
glossary.said: This is different than a scalp or directional trade

glossary.plain: A scheduled release that resolves one way or the other, earnings above all. You cannot read direction into it, so he will not carry a credit spread through one.
glossary.said: you've got a binary event you don't know which way the stock's gonna go

insights.title: The callout is deliberately incomplete, for legal reasons
insights.body: He strips strike and expiration out of every posted idea because he expects the SEC to move on Discord trading groups, and wants the group to survive by not issuing instructions. That is why the whole lesson exists: the callout is half a trade and the member supplies the other half.
insights.said: I know at some point the SEC is gonna start cracking down on these groups

insights.title: Missing a trade costs nothing
insights.body: His answer to the anxiety behind limit-versus-market. The market is not scarce — there are twelve thousand securities and the next setup is coming. The cost of chasing is real and the cost of missing is zero.
insights.said: don't ever chase a move. Don't be too anxious

insights.title: Three price targets before you enter
insights.body: He wants three targets off the chart before the trade, not one, so the trade is worth the time it takes. Notice what this replaces: he has targets for being right and nothing at all for being wrong.
insights.said: I typically wanna have three price targets when I'm taking a move because I wanna make it worth my time

insights.title: Options cut both ways at the same speed
insights.body: The reason he caps size on short expirations. The same leverage that builds an account quickly erases principal just as quickly, and the speed is the point rather than the direction.
insights.said: this can erase principle in your account extremely fast, just like it can create principle

insights.title: A spread is what you take when you cannot read the tape
insights.body: He chooses the Apple spread specifically because support has been dented but not broken and he cannot tell whether institutions are accumulating or distributing. The structure is a response to uncertainty, not to a signal — which is a more honest use of an options strategy than most.
insights.said: I'm not sure if institutions are buying or selling at this point so I don't want to take as much risk

insights.title: Round numbers matter because traders believe they do
insights.body: He picks 160 as the short leg partly because it is round. The reasoning is reflexive rather than technical — options traders cluster at round strikes, so the liquidity and the reaction are both there.
insights.said: which is also a round number options traders like round numbers

call.instrument_class: OPTIONS on single stocks (NVDA, META, MSFT). Not futures. Everything here is 2024 options.

call.note: THIS IS THE CLASS THE CALLOUTS LESSON DEFERRED TO. Two days later, in How to Use a Call-Out, Jason says 'I'll go over more in depth on a credit spread class and on a debit spread class'. This is that class, recorded two days BEFORE it.

rules.rule: On a debit spread, the risk is what you pay. Full stop.
rules.why: He says it twice in a row and then repeats it a third time — the only thing in the corpus he emphasises that hard. Pay $1,000, risk $1,000. Buying the call outright at $25 would have risked $2,500. The spread is what converts an open-ended cost into a known one.
rules.scope: OPTIONS, April 2024. This is a property of the spread structure, not a position-sizing rule, and it says nothing about futures.

rules.rule: Anytime you sell an option, that is where you cap your profit — so sell it at a resistance or support area.
rules.why: The whole trade-off in one line. In his NVDA example the stock exceeded his 828 target by $12 and he got none of it, because he had sold the 830.

rules.rule: On the short leg you want price to finish just beyond your strike, not far beyond it.
rules.why: Selling the 800 put, he wants the stock to finish above 800 but as close to 800 as possible — that is where the full premium is collected without exercise.

rules.rule: Wait for the first resistance to be hit before taking a credit spread.
rules.why: He names this as the specific mistake people make — entering while the stock is still 'no man's land' and getting hit because the first real resistance had not been tested yet.

rules.rule: A hammer candle needs another hammer candle to invalidate the move.
rules.why: A rare explicit invalidation from Jason, and it is candle-based rather than price-based. He pairs it with a confirmation candle to call the break.

rules.rule: Close the whole spread rather than legging out of one side.
rules.why: You can close the short leg and ride the long one, but that means taking the risk of a reversal naked. Closing the entire spread is 'the smarter thing to do'.

rules.rule: Use the trade for the intention you opened it for.
rules.why: His stated discipline against a spread quietly becoming a directional bet because one leg looked good.

rules.rule: Buy more time on debit spreads; keep credit spreads short so theta works for you.
rules.why: Debit out to the monthly (he uses the 17th); credit he may want expiring that Friday. On NVDA he goes long-dated either way because it makes $500-$1,500 moves on the contract price and he wants the ability to swing.

rules.rule: Draw your lines from the previous day's close.
rules.why: Asked directly how he gets his levels. The previous day close is his anchor, and he notes it was resistance-turned-support before.

rules.rule: If a stock has dropped a lot, use put credit spreads or debit call spreads — because you are looking to go long.
rules.why: His stated selector between structures. The direction of the recent move decides which side you sell premium on.

rules.rule: Spreads work best on slower movers.
rules.why: Apple or Microsoft suit spreads far better than NVDA, which he calls an anomaly at $30-40 of range a day. He uses spreads intraday on the fast ones and to swing on the slow ones.

setups.invalidation: NOT GIVEN as a price for the spread itself. The trade-level invalidation he does give is the hammer rule — a second hammer candle invalidates the move.
setups.timeframe: he uses 1h, 4h or daily for spreads
setups.numbers: 30-point spread = $3,000 of width (30 × 100 shares). Paid ~$10 = $1,000. Max profit $2,000, max loss $1,000.

Anchor your lines on the previous day's close, then read where it was resistance-turned-support.
Set the price target off the chart — the top of the previous day's candle, or the next resistance area.
Buy the strike at your entry, sell the strike at your target. The width times 100 is the spread size and the margin needed.
Choose expiration by structure: longer for debit so the move has time, shorter for credit so theta works for you.
For a credit spread, wait for the first real resistance to be tested before entering.

questions.q: Do any of these structures exist in futures?
questions.why: Spreads are an options construct. Josh trades ES. Nothing in this class transfers directly, and Jason has never bridged the two — but the level-drawing, target-setting and 'wait for first resistance' discipline arguably do.

questions.q: What is the hammer-candle rule in full?
questions.why: 'When I get a hammer candle, I need another hammer candle to invalidate the move' is one of very few explicit invalidations Jason has given, and it is stated in passing during a live class. glossary.plain: You buy the nearer option and sell a further one in the same direction. It costs money up front — it debits your account — and caps both your loss and your gain.

glossary.plain: You sell the nearer option and buy a further one for protection. Money comes in up front. He uses them because 'at the end of the day, it puts money in my account'.

glossary.plain: The distance between your two strikes, times 100 shares per contract. Buying the 800 and selling the 830 is 30 points, so $3,000 of width — and on a credit spread that width is the margin you must have.

glossary.plain: The daily decay of an option's value as expiration approaches. On a credit spread you want it working for you, which is why he keeps those shorter-dated.
glossary.said: credit spreads, you want theta to work for you

glossary.plain: When the option you sold gets used against you because price finished on the wrong side of the strike. On a credit spread that is the outcome you are avoiding.
glossary.said: When you sell an option on the bottom, you don't want it to get exercised

glossary.plain: A candle with a long lower wick and a small body — buyers rejected the low. He treats it as a reversal signal, and requires a second hammer to invalidate the move it starts.
glossary.said: when I get a hammer candle, I need another hammer candle to invalidate the move

glossary.plain: Two candles with matching lows side by side, marking a level buyers defended twice.
glossary.said: Tweezer bottom. That right there retested.

glossary.plain: Selling an option without the protective long leg. Unlimited risk on the call side. He mentions he would sometimes do it in his own trading but deliberately did not for the class.
glossary.said: Or I may sell them naked. But to be safe, I went out of the money for you guys.

glossary.plain: His term for the fact that a move is never a straight line. A stock trending down still pops back up repeatedly, and those pops cost you value while you wait — which is part of why he uses spreads intraday.
glossary.said: a lot of times markets will have ebbs and flows. This stock doesn't go straight down.

insights.title: The risk is what you pay
insights.body: The single most repeated line in the class, said three times in nine seconds. A debit spread turns an open-ended cost into a known number before you enter. It is the closest thing to a risk framework Jason has ever articulated — and it is structural rather than behavioural: the protection comes from how the trade is built, not from a stop or a rule about when to get out.
insights.said: Let me say it one more time, the risk is what you pay

insights.title: Selling is what caps you, so sell where you would have exited anyway
insights.body: His NVDA spread capped at 830 and the stock ran $12 past it — money he simply did not get. The lesson is not that capping is bad, it is that the short strike should sit where the chart says the move ends. Sell into resistance on the call side, into support on the put side.
insights.said: anytime you sell an option, that's where you cap your profit... So you wanna sell your option in a resistance area or a support area

insights.title: The mistake is entering before the first resistance is tested
insights.body: He names the specific way people lose on credit spreads: opening while the stock is still in no-man's-land, before the first real resistance has been hit. 'Somebody's gonna get hit on these because they didn't wait.' The discipline is not about the structure at all — it is about patience, and it rhymes with his 'never chase a move' rule from two days later.
insights.said: This is where people go wrong. They start taking a credit spread here when stock's in no man's land

insights.title: Sell premium on one side to finance a directional bet on the other
insights.body: He sells a 435 put, collects the premium, and uses it to buy a directional call. The same idea appears in the callouts lesson as a credit spread financing a debit spread. It is the most advanced idea in either lesson and he passes over it in a sentence.
insights.said: I may sell 435 put... So I can sell that and I can go buy directional call with that premium

insights.title: Match the structure to how fast the stock moves
insights.body: NVDA at $30-40 of daily range is 'kind of an anomaly' — he trades those intraday. Slower names like Apple and Microsoft are where spreads work properly for a swing. It is a genuinely useful selector and the only place in the corpus he ties instrument behaviour to trade structure.
insights.said: Nvidia is kind of an anomaly because it moves 30 to 40 bucks a day

insights.title: This is what a live session actually looks like
insights.body: Unlike every polished lesson in the corpus, this one has him fighting his screen share, losing his place, saying 'not sure what's going on on my screen here, but whatever', and answering attendees mid-thought. Useful context for Josh: the real classes are messier than the tutorials, and the good material arrives in fragments.
